5. Topology

Open sets, compactness, completeness — the topology of the real line, the Baire category theorem, Cantor sets.

  • Open and Closed Sets — A set UUU is open when every point is an interior point — each point can be wrapped in an ε\varepsilonε-ball. Move the point xxx and the radius ε\varepsilonε on the line and watch whether the ball stays inside.
  • Clopen Sets — Sets that are both open and closed — clopen. In R\mathbb{R}R only ∅\varnothing∅ and R\mathbb{R}R qualify (proved in full), but change the ambient space and the same set's fate changes: [0,1][0,1][0,1] is merely closed in R\mathbb{R}R, yet clopen inside [0,1]∪[2,3][0,1]\cup[2,3][0,1]∪[2,3].
  • Closure and Boundedness — Drawing a bar over AAA gives the closure A‾\overline{A}A — the set with its escaped limit points pulled back in. Follow the round-song: closed ⟺ contains its limit points ⟺ equals its closure, and closed + bounded ⟺ compact (Heine-Borel).
  • Compact Sets — Compact   ⟺  \iff⟺ closed + bounded (Heine–Borel): [0,1][0,1][0,1] is covered by the first 6 intervals of its open cover, while (0,1](0,1](0,1] fails at the gap near 0 and [0,∞)[0,\infty)[0,∞) fails at the infinite tail. Sequential compactness via Bolzano–Weierstrass is proved in full; the open-cover definition's equivalence is shown at the idea level.
  • Topologist's Sine Curve — The closure of {(x,sin⁡(1/x)):x>0}\{(x, \sin(1/x)) : x > 0\}{(x,sin(1/x)):x>0} adds the segment {0}×[−1,1]\{0\}\times[-1,1]{0}×[−1,1] on the yyy-axis. Connected as the closure of a connected set, yet no path runs from the segment into the curve — the living example of why connected is weaker than path-connected.
  • Peano Curve — A continuous map [0,1]→[0,1]2[0,1] \to [0,1]^2[0,1]→[0,1]2 can fill the whole square — recursively repeating the 9-subsquare snake yields uniformly convergent approximations with a surjective continuous limit. Injectivity is impossible (Netto's theorem, proved in full).
  • Metric Spaces — Axiomatizing distance generalizes the ε\varepsilonε-ball — the shape of an open ball B(c,r)B(c, r)B(c,r) depends on the metric ddd. Compare the Euclidean disk, the max-norm square, and the extreme discrete metric.
  • Contraction Mapping Principle — A contraction d(Tx,Ty)≤q d(x,y)d(Tx,Ty) \le q\,d(x,y)d(Tx,Ty)≤qd(x,y) (q<1q<1q<1) on a complete metric space has a unique fixed point — the Picard iterates xn+1=Txnx_{n+1} = Tx_nxn+1​=Txn​ tighten inside the error ball qn1−q∣x1−x0∣\frac{q^n}{1-q}|x_1-x_0|1−qqn​∣x1​−x0​∣. T(x)=x/2T(x) = x/2T(x)=x/2 on (0,1](0,1](0,1] shows why completeness is essential: a contraction with no fixed point.
  • Baire Category Theorem — A complete metric space cannot be a countable union of nowhere dense sets — that is the Baire Category Theorem. Dodging the rationals of [0,1][0, 1][0,1] one by one with nested closed intervals IkI_kIk​ leaves a single irrational point in the intersection, whose lengths shrink to 000.
  • Baire Class 1 Functions — Pointwise limits of continuous functions — Baire class 1. Thomae's function T(p/q)=1/qT(p/q) = 1/qT(p/q)=1/q (reduced), T(x)=0T(x) = 0T(x)=0 (irrational) is the pointwise limit of sums fnf_nfn​ of disjoint tents. TTT is continuous at irrationals, discontinuous at rationals — a living example of Baire's theorem that the continuity points contain a dense GδG_\deltaGδ​.
  • Length Zero, Points Uncountable — Deleting middle thirds drives the total length (23)n→0\left(\frac{2}{3}\right)^n\to 0(32​)n→0, yet uncountably many points remain. Uncountability is stated at the idea level only.
  • The Fat Cantor Set — What if we dig out less? Removing only length 4−n4^{-n}4−n per interval leaves a set that is compact, nowhere dense and perfect — yet keeps total length 12\frac1221​. Measure and topological size are independent notions.
  • The Cantor Function — The Devil's staircase: continuous and nondecreasing from 000 to 111, yet constant on every complementary interval, so f′=0f' = 0f′=0 on a set of total length 111. f(1)−f(0)=1≠∫01f′f(1) - f(0) = 1 \neq \int_0^1 f'f(1)−f(0)=1=∫01​f′ — why the FTC needs more than differentiability almost everywhere.
